title: Triple treble
subtitle: An extra-tall lace stitch, called double treble in the United States
excerpt: The triple treble is taller still, made with three yarn-overs and worked off in four steps. It is a specialist lace stitch: the long posts that span wide gaps in openwork, fans, and the deep points of edgings.
sourceNotes: Reconstructed in our own words from Thérèse de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), Chapter 9 (Crochet Work), the passage describing the taller trebles worked with additional wraps, the family of long stitches that follows the double treble. Public domain via Project Gutenberg. UK and US stitch-name equivalences cross-checked against the Craft Yarn Council standard terms.

glossaryTerms.definition: An extra-tall crochet stitch made with three yarn-overs before the hook goes in, then worked off two loops at a time in four steps. The UK name; called double treble in the United States.
The United States name for the stitch British patterns call a triple treble. The steps are identical; only the name differs by one place along the scale of stitch heights.
Wrapping the working yarn over the hook from back to front before working a stitch. A triple treble takes three wraps before the hook goes in.

content.text: The
triple treble
carries the family of tall stitches one step further. You begin with three wraps of
yarn round hook

, then work the loops off two at a time over four steps. The post is long and the stitch grows tall fast, which is exactly what wide lace and deep-pointed edgings need. In the United States this stitch is called
double treble
, one name lower than the British scale, so the count of wraps matters more than the name.
How to form the stitch
Begin with one working loop on the hook.
Wrap the yarn over the hook three times.
Insert the hook into the next stitch or chain.
Wrap the yarn over and draw a loop back through. Five loops sit on the hook.
Wrap the yarn over and pull through two loops. Four loops remain.
Wrap the yarn over and pull through two more. Three loops remain.
Wrap the yarn over and pull through two more. Two loops remain.
Wrap the yarn over and pull through the last two. One loop is left, and the triple treble is done.
At the start of a row, five chains stand in for the first triple treble.
Where you will use it

Triple trebles appear where a pattern needs real height: the long spokes of a round doily, the deep points of a lace edging, the tall sides of an openwork fan. They span a wide gap in a single stitch, which lets lace patterns leap across open ground. You will meet them mostly in Victorian-style edgings and fine thread work rather than everyday garments.
Variations and related stitches

Each extra wrap at the start adds another two-loop pull and another post-height, so the same method makes quadruple trebles and beyond for the deepest lace. The double treble is the shorter neighbour. Worked in clusters the triple treble makes tall, dramatic fans. Keeping the wraps loose as you begin stops the final pulls from fighting you.
Difficulty: intermediate. The motion repeats a familiar pattern; the only challenge is keeping count of the pull-throughs.
